desc:
When the wind comes from the east these fields are sprayed with a gentle mist
from the Anduin. Even as the wind seize, the dew holds firmly to the swaying
grass, with never-ending moisture. In the west a mossy wall of trees grows
closely together, clinging to each other in the mossy ground as if to avoid
sinking into the earth. Some of the trees have immigrated into these fields, but
the rest quickly turn away in the north and south.
name: Moist Plain at the Anduin

desc:
Following the shores of the Anduin to the south, these fields get cornered in by
the border of the Gladden Fields and the steep banks of the Great River. The
earth is damp and moist, but the grey moss of the west has not completely filled
the plains. The rain that falls gets transported either into the swampy grounds
in the west, or the river in the east. This leaves the ground with a healthy
moisture giving place for flowers and fragile stems of grass. To the west a
sharp slippery decline leads into the marsh.
name: Border of the Gladden Fields

desc:
Cramped in between the Anduin and the Gladden Fields, these fields are covered
in a gentle mist. The roaring of the Great River rushes over the plains, and a
strong scent of decay flows in from the west. Yellow flowers grow in patches,
and in the west sturdy grey grass decorates the border of the marshes. A sharp
drop into the marsh makes travelling this way impossible.
name: Watery Fields

desc:
Yellow patches of gentle flowers spot the land, spreading out in the grass that
still stands tall in the soft ground. The rushing sound of the Anduin flows in
over the lands, and its sparkling flow glitters in the south-east. Sturdy grey
stems of grass grow in row after row at the border of the Gladden in the west,
and a sharp slippery decline leads into the soggy marsh.
name: Damp Fields of Hay

desc:
Dead rotting branches of the brush reach in from the north. The ground has
become soft and soggy, and unusable for the woody stems of bushes and tangles
that try to complete their ruling of the lands. Orange grass still sways gently
in the plains, but the earth is spotted with moss and lichen.
name: Dying Tangles

desc:
Green and flourishing, these fields lie snugly in a valley at the turn of the
Anduin in the east and south. The Great River's rushing water echoes over the
land. The ground is soft and wet, caused by the close relation to the flowing
water, but the level earth serves as good growth place for grass and flowers.
Close in the north a large gathering of rocks and debris has been gathered next
to a few sturdy pines, forming a moderately concealed hovel in the field.
Peaking out from the top, a column of rocks and crudely cut boards form a watch
tower, not higher then the trees next to it, but protected with a slanting roof
and walls in all directions.
name: Concealed Camp at the Anduin

desc:
Not far in the east the gentle murmur of the Anduin current echoes through the
land. These fields are once in a while filled with the rising water as the
bending river sometimes cannot follow its destined path. Rain and dew also
choose these fields as a course towards the flowing water of the Anduin. This
results in a soft and muddy field sparsely filled with swaying hay and the
shrubs reaching in from the north rotting away in the mist. In the south a rocky
mound blocks the path along the river.
name: Misty Shores

desc:
Clusters of blueberries grow among the rocks and short birches here. The ground
is hard and covered by dry leaves, sticks and splinters of wood which form neat
lines along the ant trails in the undergrowth. The highest point in these dry
fields, an outcrop of bare rock, is surrounded by a carpet of moss and stunted
conifer trees.
name: A Patch of Blueberries

desc:
A carpet of grass and tiny flowers covers the ground here, just above the cliffs
that border the riverbed of the Anduin. The ridge starts from the river's edge
and continues to the east, where the vegetation seems to get taller. One could
have a good look over the river from this open field, but one would also be in
danger of being spotted oneself.
name: Riverside Fields above a Cliff

desc:
The small dirt path running through the fields and shrubberies here does not
look like it was made by animals. After following it for a while, a pair of boot
prints, preserved in the hardened mud, can be noticed. Their size is quite
small, but the tracks are too old to tell who passed through here. In the
northwest, lush fields spread out towards the river, while in the opposite
direction tall bushes dominate the landscape.
name: A Footpath through the Fields

desc:
Round shrubs with large leaves grow in tightly packed groups here and there,
covering this dry field. The ground declines slightly to the southeast, but
moving that way seems as hard as going in any other direction; the paths amidst
the shrubbery twist and bend as they lead through the narrow openings between
bushes. A wider path, covered in grass and loose stones, leads through the field
as it follows the direction of the slope.
name: A Shrub-covered Field

desc:
The bank of the river has turned into a landslide where roots and vegetation
failed to hold the sand in place. In many spots the grassy mat suddenly ends at
the waters edge, and a steep embankment of loose soil leads down to the river
instead. A small path follows the course of the river here, and then disappears
into the grass.
name: Steep Banks of the Anduin

desc:
Small ponds and puddles of water break the monotony of these wet plains near the
banks of the Anduin. Clusters of irises and reeds thrive in the shallow waters,
and tall weeds cover the higher grounds. A stretch of rocky fields farther away
from the river offers an easier route through the plains, reaching from the
riverside in the north to the sloping grounds in the south.
name: Wetlands near the River

desc:
This secluded valley seems to be teeming with life; here and there one can catch
glimpses of small animals' tracks and tunnels amidst the thriving undergrowth.
Starting from a spring near the ridge in the north, a small stream runs down to
the bottom of the valley, where it quickly soaks into the ground; there it
serves to nourish the thick clusters of various plants. Rocky fields separate
this area of lush vegetation from the riverside wetlands in the west.
name: A Small Valley

desc:
Here, a gentle slope rises towards the high hills in the south. Stunted trees
and bushes grow in some places, but there is a clear line of sight almost all
the way down to the wide plains in the north and east. Moving along the hillside
seems rather easy, and many paths lie open to travellers; paths leading past
rocky outcroppings and dry fields.
name: Gently Sloping Hillside

desc:
There seems to be no end to these plains. While looking over yet another grassy
ridge, all one can see is sloping ground that spreads out towards the horizon.
Travelling to the north seems easier than to the other directions, since going
that way is mostly downhill. Luckily, there are several animal paths to help a
traveller maintain his direction on the way through this featureless landscape.
name: Undulating Plains

desc:
The grass grows high and thick here, covering most of the land. In the west the
sparkle of the Anduin river reflects in the fields, the furious sound of its
rushing water echoes even this far away. Bare scraped branches of small bushes
and trampled flowers witness a great deal of activity here. Food is plentiful
for the animals, and water can be found only a couple of miles to the west in
the clear current of the Anduin.
name: Fields of Green

desc:
The ground on the bottom of this depression is muddy and it looks like it may be
sinking down. Roots and loosely hanging branches of the tall bushes growing here
hinder movement in most places, while the plains surrounding the hollow seem to
offer easier paths for travellers. A puddle of water in the middle of this
depression is full of rotting leaves and moss; the field is slowly turning into
a peat bog.
name: A Bushy Hollow

desc:
These sparsely wooded ridges offers good viewpoints over the plains for anyone
willing to climb up the ridge here. A mounted traveller, however, would have no
choice but to ride through the fields below the ridges, where the terrain seems
perfect for setting up ambushes or lookouts. Decent paths are nowhere to be
found, yet the old remains of a campsite among some rocks suggest that someone
passes through here occasionally.
name: Ridged Plains

desc:
In the surrounding areas, with the Anduin in the west and the Gladden stretching
beyond it, are plains upon plains. This patch of hills stands out as a break in
the lands. To the east the hills stretch a bit further, but quickly flatten out
again. In the south a small forest grows on the feet of the hills. The ground is
still covered with thick grass, but on some of the slopes rocks and gravel have
been left bare under the sky.
name: Flowing Hills

desc:
The hills in the north quickly flatten out here making room for trees to gather
and form a colony next to the Anduin. The ground is soft and mossy, watered by
the Anduin and numerous stains of water, gathered in pools beneath the trees.
The trees themselves are covered in moss and lichen, and many have started to
decay, rotting away in the wet climate.
name: Mossy Forest

desc:
With the ground being raised slightly higher than the northern forest, this area
is rather safe from the Anduin, which flows to the north-west. The bottoms of
the tree trunks are covered by some green moss and some rotten branches can be
seen among the fallen leaves.
name: A Slightly Wet Forest

desc:
The ground, bearing patches of fallen leaves, is rather flat here, except in the
south where it transforms into low slopes. The forest, mix of beeches and oaks,
continues in all the directions, although only the northern part remains
somewhat dense.
name: A Mixed Forest

desc:
The earth of these tree-covered slopes seems to be mixed with quite some large
and irregular pebbles. To the south, the relief increases considerably, where
most of the trees have faded and are finally leaving the place to a tall, rather
bare hill. However, the hill can barely be noticed, through the thinner parts of
the surrounding forest.
name: Woody Slopes

desc:
The Anduin River borders to the west of this rather thin and mixed forest, which
then thickens to the east. There is some relief, slight mounds and depressions
here and there, however insignificant compared to the southern small and wooded
hills.
name: A Forest Bordering the Anduin

desc:
Small, thorny thickets are growing here and there, raising the relief of this
otherwise rather flat riverbank, save from its south-eastern part maybe. It is
bordered to the northwest by the Anduin, where some relatively small trees can
also be found, especially near the eastern forest.
name: A Woody Riverbank

desc:
Groups of young oaks and rowans stand out on these windswept hilltops. More
trees can be seen in the south, where dense bushes border the outskirts of a
forest. Bare outcrops of rock and fields of small flowers fill the hollows
between the hills, while in the east a steep slope leads down to a patch of
thick vegetation and grassy fields.
name: Sparsely Wooded Hills

desc:
The slim trunks of the young trees that grow here bend slightly whenever there
is a gust of wind. Brown leaves, fallen from the rowans and birches during last
autumn, still cling to the twigs that stick out among the mossy rocks and
stumps. The ground is damp, and the soil is bare near a spot where a large
animal has been digging for roots or mushrooms to eat.
name: Outskirts of a Forest

desc:
These small hills, some only being low mounds, slightly rise up southwards. As
they do, they appear to slowly lose their trees, finally matching the bare and
low eminences that are visible in this direction. Westwards, they slowly fade
into a rather bare and flat plain.
name: Forested Hills

desc:
While there are wild weeds and grasses in growth upon the front of the southern
hill, no thorn can be distinguished among them. The hill itself appears to be
part of a larger portion of hills, ranging to the south. The nearest slope is
nearly vertical and completely covered by climbing weeds.
name: Grassland in Front of a Hill

desc:
Taller hills overlook these lower ones from the west and east. All the nearby
slopes are pretty steep, each covered by a slippery moss, making climbing the
slopes to be nearly impossible. Besides reaching the forested hills that are to
the north, it appears the terrain is safe to move southwards, along the flat
parts between the slopes.
name: Low Hills

desc:
The western slope of this tall hill, rather tight and slippery, leads to a sea
of steep mounds, that is much darker than their surroundings. Though nearly
vertical, the northern incline appears possible to climb down using the large
and numerous stones that have been partly embedded in the earth.
name: A Tall Hill

desc:
Unlike the similar mounds that are visible westwards, to the east stands a tall,
green hill, having a top that is seemingly strewn with small bushes. While the
slippery vegetable matter covering all of the area nearly prevents anyone from
climbing any of the slopes, a safe and flat path can be found towards the south
and the north.
name: Among the Hills

desc:
This tall hill is easily reachable from the northern one, by following a common,
curved crest. While the western slope is rather steep and slippery, leading to a
lower and natural eminence, the southern landscape is made of plains. They
appear to be reachable by a bush-covered incline.
name: A Tall Hill

desc:
The earth in this area is very slick and the thin, wet moss that has grown on
the surrounding slopes does not make their climb less dangerous. The flat path
between the hills quickly stops east after a few of dead-ends, while the
southern one is blocked by a long mound.
name: Among the Hills

desc:
The hills here are rather small, but their slopes are steep and slippery. It is
possible to safely walk and ride between them to the east and south, judging by
its appearance. Besides a few dead-ends, there is no safe passage visible that
leads northwards towards the higher hills. The tops of the trees of a forest are
noticed behind the western hills.
name: Among the Hills

desc:
The slopes of these small hills are slippery and very tight, causing them to be
very difficult to climb. The bottom of the slopes between the hills, while
strewn with sharp protruding rocks, appears to be rather safe. A somewhat usable
path can be found towards the north and the south.
name: Among the Hills

desc:
The hills here are much smaller than the ones that can be seen northwards in the
distance. Their slopes are less steep, especially the one which leads to a lone,
large mound to the south. The trees appear to border this range of hills in both
directions to the west and east.
name: Small Hills

desc:
Unlike the northern hills, this tall one is reachable using easy slopes. While
the eastern slope soon transforms into a slightly wooded area, a similar mound
can be seen westwards. However, the western eminence is lacking the several
shrubs that are growing atop of this one. Distinguished among these are many
boulders, partly buried into the ground.
name: Hill Overlooking a Trail

desc:
The beech-covered, wide mounds that slightly hinder the movement in this area
are quite flat, compared to the tall hill that stands westwards and is visible
through the thinner parts of the surrounding foliage of the trees. Although the
bottom of some of the depressions is wet, no moss that can be seen grows on the
base of the trunks.
name: Woody Hills

desc:
While it is possible to follow the crests to reach the northern hills, among
which a taller one stands out, the eastern and southern surroundings consist of
quite smaller hills. The small hills are separated from the rest by very tight
and mossy slopes. The western, woody slope leads to a thin forest.
name: Among the Hills

desc:
While the northern landscapes are rather flat, save from a small forest in the
north-east, it becomes a sea of hills south from here. The nearby hills to the
west and south from are continuous enough, that it is possible to reach them
without having to climb much. However, the hills in the east are pretty small
and only reachable by a tight, slippery slope.
name: On the Top of a Hill

desc:
This old trail can be guessed to meet the Anduin, which is several miles to the
west, but it is hard to tell whether it ever reaches the shadows of Mirkwood to
the far east. Its slabs have been laid on the lower part of the gentle slope of
the northern hill. Some of the slabs have been broken by whatever has travelled
upon them.
name: Ancient Trail

desc:
This old trail appears to follow a vague west-east direction, however entire
parts of it have disappeared. The used slabs have either been looted or maybe
simply buried under the vegetable matter over the time. There are some small
trees, probably the result of the nearby, northern forest which appears to
further dislocate the path.
name: Ancient Trail by a Wood

desc:
The nearby mounds and depressions are easily noticeable, even through the forest
that is surrounding them. While most of the forest consists of beech trees, a
few weeds are strewn over the rough mix of earth and angular pebbles. While the
relief is less visible to the north, a whole range of steep hills stands to the
west.
name: Woody Hills

desc:
The hills here are rather low and would actually be better described as a
succession of mounds and depressions. The soil is grassy and mixed with some
irregular pebbles. There are also some lonely trees, probably the offspring of
the southern forest, which can be seen marking the landscape here and there.
name: Approach of the Hills

desc:
The accentuated relief of the plain here nearly hinders travel, however, it is
still easy to avoid the steepest slopes. While patches of mild bushes are in
growth among the flat parts, none of this vegetation has grown above the size of
an average shrub.
name: An Uneven Plain

desc:
While these plains are somewhat uneven, made so by small mounds of earth, their
slopes seem no taller than the short bushes that have been strewn over the rest
of the land. There are some rare pebbles that are visible through the thinner
parts of the grass layer which completely covers the soil.
name: Plains near a Small Forest

desc:
The bottoms of all the slight depressions here on this somewhat, uneven plain
are too muddy to contain any drinkable water. It is, however, well enough to
allow a luxuriant vegetation to grow, parasite weeds covering the grass, a
lonely boulder and the trunks of the few trees that grow here.
name: Plains near a Small Forest

desc:
The old slabs of this part of the ancient trail appear to have remained in a
somewhat decent shape, covered only by weeds and vegetable matter. The road,
bending to the south, is breaking its relatively straight course coming from the
west, but soon it looks to change its direction once again.
name: A Bend in an Ancient Trail

desc:
Mounds and terrain depressions strew this uneven plain, however, they are not
tall enough to hinder movement. Some high grasses of some sort are covering
everything, their monotony broken here and there by a dark bush or a partly
buried boulder. A range of steep hills border the area to the west.
name: An Uneven Plain

desc:
Growing near a range of hills in the west, this brushwood comprised of young
trees and bushes is slowly turning into a forest. Many of the oaks are already
taller than most Men, and slender birches have sprouted out among them during
the past few summers. Some older trees can be seen to the southwest, where a
forest continues towards the hilltops. Wide, grassy plains spread out away from
the hills as far as the eye can see.
name: A Small Coppice at the Hillside

desc:
Small dirt paths, covered in old animal tracks, lead through the plains towards
areas of vegetation in the north and in the west. High hay covers the ground
here, and the tops of bushes and saplings that grows here and there have been
chewed off by deer or other large animals. In some places, tiny tufts of
feathers or fur stick to the hardy straws near the ground, hinting at the fact
that a multitude of small animals live in these fields.
name: Animal Paths

desc:
A smooth carpet of grass covers these slopes and fields, creating an unbroken
surface that seems to continue very far in every direction. Even rocks and
bushes are scarce here, and those that can be found are far too small to provide
cover for anyone but the tiniest animals. A single animal path leads to the
northeast, however, and the thickening vegetation suggests that water might be
found in that direction.
name: Grassy Plains

desc:
A wooded ridge, shaped like a crescent moon, separates this dry field from the
bordering plains. Dense brushwood surrounds the field completely, leaving only
one opening at the side of the ridge where passing through is easier. A huge log
has been dragged to the middle of the field where it serves as a bench; the
circle of sooty stones lying in front of the log seems to have held campfires in
the past. At the inner side of the ridge, an entrance to a small cave lies
almost hidden by a pair of bushes.
name: A Campsite amidst a Brushwood

desc:
Wind, rain and a lack of vegetation have turned this part of the plains into a
bare field of soil and gravel. Hardy weeds and twigs cling to sheltered spots
near some larger rocks, but other than that the landscape is completely barren.
A dry streambed leads to the west, towards areas where bushes thrive among
richer soil.
name: A Gravelly Field

desc:
The gravelly remains of a trail leads westwards, past meadows and small stands
of trees, towards a field of shrubs. In the east, the trail becomes too
overgrown to follow, and it ends near a lonely elm that stands upon a hillock. A
narrow ditch following the trail bends to the north, where it too gets engulfed
by dense vegetation under a gentle slope.
name: Remnants of a Trail

desc:
Large rocks covered by mosses and lichen stand in this field of dry hay. The
ground slopes up towards a stand of young trees in the west and down towards
grassy fields in other directions. The high hay conceals some smaller rocks,
which might make movement without stumbling over them hard, but would also
provide cover for small animals scurrying from one hiding place to another.
name: A Rocky Slope

desc:
Two sooty walls built of logs are all that remains standing of this destroyed
farmhouse. There seems to have been a fire; the bark on the trees near the house
is somewhat charred and piles of blackened debris lie near the walls. The house
also had a fireplace and a chimney, but of those only a pile of rubble remains.
Stinging nettles and other tall plants thrive in the rich soil among the ruins.
name: A Ruined Farmhouse

desc:
Waist-high rocks, covered in lichen, and young trees growing in thick clusters
hinder movement on the bottom of this small valley situated between the slopes
in the north and in the south. The grassy plains extending to the west gradually
turn into heathlands here, and the hardy weeds are replaced by evergreen sprigs
bearing berries of many different colours. In the east, the vale ends in a
sparsely wooded heath.
name: Heathlands at the Edge of Fields

desc:
Tussocks of yellowed grass and weeds cover the bumps and depressions in these
treeless fields. The ground is dry and sandy, but it appears even more so in the
east where the fields slowly turn into a sparsely wooded heath. In some places,
a bare field of sand with no vegetation other than the occasional tufts of grass
spreads out. Any tracks would be clearly visible there, if the wind did not wipe
them out regularly.
name: Bumpy, Dry Fields

desc:
An outcrop of rock, shaped like a giant clenched fist, breaks the monotony of
the fields spreading out everywhere around it. The ground slopes steeply upwards
in the east, where a clear path leads around the ledge to the fields above.
Boulders about the size of a pony lie scattered around the outcrop, while
smaller ones dot the fields in the west.
name: Under a Rocky Ledge

desc:
The bedrock is quite close to the surface here, since masses of bare rock stick
out of the dry fields of hay in some places. In the west, a rocky ledge breaks
the grassy slope leading to the plains below, but there seems to be a path going
around it. The few trees growing above the ledge are stunted; a small wood of
birches stands much farther away, thriving in the rich soil of the moors that
extend to the east.
name: Dry Fields above a Ledge

desc:
The high, yellowed hay growing in these windswept fields rustles quietly even
when the air stands still. Cracks run through the dry mud in places where the
water formed puddles during last rains, and the ground is hard like rock in most
places. Small piles of fist-sized stones can be seen among the hay near the
rockier grounds in the east; grooves in the sand amidst the stones hint at the
presence of small rodents, lizards or even snakes.
name: Dry Fields of Hay

desc:
Tall thistles with thorny leaves and stems grow among the grass in these
undulating fields. There are no clear paths through the vegetation, and in some
places the tangled grass and plants have grown tall enough to stick to boots and
legs, making movement hard. Some boulders stand in the fields, half hidden by
grass and thistles, and much more than just rocks might lie unseen in the
undergrowth. While standing, however, one can be seen from afar, since there are
hardly any trees or large bushes growing in these fields.
name: Thistles in the Grass

desc:
Here, a peaceful meadow of flowers spreads out under a huge willow. A pile of
large, round stones stands under the tree; the stones are sandy and brown, as if
they were dug out of the ground only recently. There are some cart tracks on the
ground, and it looks like the stones were brought here instead of having been
gathered in the immediate surroundings. A small path leads to the north, where a
thick growth of stinging nettles separates this meadow from what seems to be a
small cabin.
name: A Small Cairn

desc:
Some hollow trunks are all that remains of a small patch of forest that once
grew here. There must be at least a dozen of these lying around on this meadow
alone, and the high hay in the south might conceal more. The trunks are very dry
and scarred, and there are small splinters and pieces of fungus on the ground.
It looks like someone has gathered a supply of touchwood here, though it could
be that these markings are made by just animals. Some living trees still stand
far away to the east.
name: Fallen Trunks

desc:
Two dead oaks stand tall in the middle of this field, surrounded by patches of
flowers. Only one crooked branch remains on the taller tree; the rest seem to
have been cracked off by strong winds and fallen into a dry tangle on the
ground. The shorter of the two trees died only recently, and caps from its last
acorns still cling to the thin branches. Grassy fields spread out in all
directions around the pair of trees.
name: A Pair of Dead Trees

desc:
Ancient stumps of what were once mighty trees stand out among the mossy rocks in
this bumpy field of hay. The thick branches that are lying on the ground are
grey and without bark on them, and it seems like the trees that grew here were
cut down many years ago. Still, there are some recent axe cuts on one stump, and
splinters lying on the ground around it; someone has been here looking for
firewood.
name: A Field of Stumps and Branches

desc:
Clusters of wild wheat grow in this smooth field. Two poles that might once have
held the hinges of a gate stand at the edge of the field - an edge where one can
also see the end of a trail. The trail leads to the east past similar fields and
overgrown pastures. No signs of cattle are visible, but some droppings on the
ground hint at game animals coming here to graze.
name: An Old Pasture

desc:
Smooth grass covers the ancient ruins of a village here. There seems to have
been at least two dozen houses built of logs, but most of their woodwork has
rotted away or slowly sunk into the ground over the years. The structures that
were built of stone stand out better; the foundation of a large hall lies in the
middle of an open field, surrounded by the other ruins. While looking into a few
spots behind the large grassy mounds that used to be houses, a collapsed
underground storage and a large stone well can be noticed among the rubble.
name: Ruins of a Village

desc:
Among the trees growing in these dry fields, someone has piled up rocks about
the size of a man's head into mounds several yards wide. Perhaps the ground was
being cleared for planting a field; perhaps the mounds were built for burial. In
any case, whatever took place here happened many years ago; some of the smaller
mounds are now almost entirely covered in grass.
name: Rocky Mounds in the Fields

desc:
The fields here are dotted by knee-high stones covered in velvety evergreen
moss. Tiny ferns clinging to the sides of the stones seem to be the only plants
thriving in these dry meadows; the grass is yellowed and all the flowers seem to
have withered away before growing to full height. A group of rowans standing on
a hillock seems to be the best landmark on the otherwise level landscape.
name: Among the Stones

desc:
Thick boards have been laid down to cover up the dirt floor of this small cabin,
but there is still bare ground near the door and around the crude stone oven
that sits in one of the corners. There is no fire in the oven right now, but the
stones are quite warm and are radiating heat into the whole building. A wooden
table and a pair of benches, carved out of huge logs, stands near the back wall.
A piece of bark attached to a metal holder is burning above the table, giving
faint light to the room. There is a rack close to the ceiling, possibly meant to
store food or supplies.
name: A Farmer's Hut

desc:
This paddock is surrounded by a sturdy wooden fence with a gate leading out to
the pastures in the west. The fence connects with the back wall of a farmhouse
in the east, where a small door leads inside. A heap of hay has been left on a
rack at one corner of the fence for the animals to eat, and there are also some
cereals from a better meal remaining on the ground. Some water is dripping to
the ground from a trough standing next to the rack.
name: An Animal Paddock

desc:
A long table, with benches lying on both sides, stands in the middle of the main
hall of this farmhouse. A wall made of huge logs separates the hall from a
cramped kitchen, while the chimney leading down through the wall turns into a
fireplace on this side and into an oven inside the kitchen. Some beds lie in the
far corner of the hall, surrounded by a curtain that can be pulled around them
for some privacy. There also seems to be a large bedroom at the end of a short
hallway near the main entrance to the house.
name: Inside a Large Farmhouse

desc:
The water on the basement floor is less than two feet deep, and a barely
noticeable current suggests that it is somehow connected to the river. The piles
of debris in the water consist of floorboards, broken cogwheels and other parts
of the old woodwork. Most of it is buried in the mud; the wood has not rotted
away over the years, but recovering any parts would be hard work. Two wooden
beams lean against the wall, making climbing in and out of the basement a bit
easier.
name: A Watery Basement

desc:
This quiet pond, surrounded by a thick shrubbery, lies here on the bottom of a
hollow in the plains. The pond is somewhat overgrown; thick growths of moss,
hardly solid enough to walk on, cover its surface near the banks, and dense
bushes makes it hard to reach the water in most places. The hollow continues to
the south, where one can spot some trees among the shrubs.
name: A Shallow Pond

desc:
The ground here seems to be too dry for most weeds and flowers, but hardy shrubs
cover the patches of sand and gravel where even the widespread carpet of grass
has died away. It seems like there have been better seasons for growth, since
many of the bushes are still quite massive. In many places they have gathered
into dense shrubberies, where small animals can seek cover from the birds of
prey that can sometimes be seen circling in the sky far above.
name: Bushy Plains

desc:
This pond of water, starts out not more than a foot or two deep here, gradually
turning into a deeper pool in the north. Thick bushes and stunted trees grow on
tussocks of grass, sinking their clumps of roots into the shallow water. While
moving around through the bushes, some empty nests among the roots can be
noticed, and branches sway in some places as if small birds were hopping on
them.
name: Bird Nests in the Bushes

desc:
Tall ferns along with round bushes with thorny branches grow in clusters in this
field of bracken. The shrubbery is most dense on the bottom of a moist
depression, which separates the sloping grounds in the southeast from the wide
plains extending to other directions. An old trunk, buried in evergreen moss,
can be seen lying among the thick ferns down there; dead leaves cover the rest
of the ground.
name: Among the Bushes and Bracken

desc:
Passing through dense growths of bushes and bracken, winding paths lead down
into this quiet hollow surrounded by brushwood and small hillocks. The slopes
that lead away from here are so steep, and the vegetation is so dense, that the
rays of the sun do not reach directly into the hollow. Everything is cloaked in
twilight; clusters of horsetails grow under the trees, covering the ground with
a feathery shroud of green and grey.
name: Horsetails in the Shade

desc:
A wide stretch of short grass leads straight to the south, through the plains.
Somehow this spot does not seem to have formed naturally; tall plants grow
everywhere in the surrounding fields except here, yet there are no signs of
cattle or anything that might rid this area of such vegetation. Perhaps the soil
is too dry or the bedrock too near for any bushes or trees to take root.
name: A Fairway through the Plains

desc:
No shelter from the wind can be found on these widespread plains of grass. In
some places the hay is lying low, flattened by the last rain, revealing rocks
and other small bumps on the ground that might have otherwise remained hidden
from sight. Keeping an eye on the features of the open sky seems to be the only
way to keep a direction while travelling through these vast plains.
name: Wide, Grassy Plains

desc:
A field of yellowed hay and tall perennial plants spreads out here. Some of the
plants have had their dry cores picked clean by local birds; others are still
spreading their seeds into the breeze. Sparse bushes grow in the north, while
the fields of hay continue to the west as well as towards the sloping grounds in
the eastern reaches of these plains.
name: High Hay

desc:
Sandy depressions break the smooth carpet of grass in many places on these
gently sloping fields. Small puddles of water have formed on the bottom of many
such hollows, and tiny tracks of birds can be noticed around them. Sparse bushes
surround the areas of sand, and there seems to be a thick shrubbery at the
bottom of the slope to the north.
name: A Gentle Slope

desc:
Some rust-coloured leaves still cling to the branches of the bushes growing
here, but much more can be found drying up on the ground. The bushes rustle
quietly in the breeze as their branches scrape against each other, with leaves
and sticks making a crackling noise underneath. Still, it seems possible to move
among the bushes undetected; even without leaves they are concealing, and it is
hard to tell if any noises are caused by anything but the wind.
name: Dry Shrubs

desc:
Moving on these sloping fields can be somewhat straining at times, but the wide
plains in the north and in the west seem to offer easier ways for travelling. A
steep slope, covered in short hay and clusters of heather, leads up to the
southeast, where the short bushes growing here are replaced by tall pine trees.
Rain water has carved sandy furrows into the ground; they lead down the slope
through the vegetation.
name: Rising Plains

desc:
The ground begins to slope gently upwards in the east, as the even, bushy plains
extending to the northwest come to an end here. The slopes are covered in short,
hardy bushes, but climbing up and down seems easy enough even without grabbing
the vegetation. A small stream, not more than two feet wide, streams in from the
east, babbling cheerfully until it gradually dries up while running towards the
bottom of the slope.
name: Grassy Slopes

desc:
The smoothly curving slope suddenly turns into an unnaturally flat terrace.
There are no signs of any recent farming in the area, but the shape of the field
and the narrow furrows running through it in neat lines suggests that many years
ago something was grown here. Currently the ground is covered in tangled vines,
thistles and small woody-stemmed shrubs, and the field does not seem readily
arable with all the roots and moss smothering the soil.
name: An Overgrown Garden

desc:
A smooth carpet of grass covers the hilltops and small valleys between them.
Travelling among the hills seems easy, even if keeping one's direction might
require climbing on a hillock and taking a look around occasionally. Nothing
taller than flowers grows on the round, windswept hilltops, and if there is any
shelter from the weather, the thick bushes enshrouding the hillsides keep it
hidden well. In the east, even taller bushes dominate the rising landscape.
name: Smooth Hills

desc:
An even meadow of tiny flowers spreads out here above the slope going down in
the north. The field is surrounded by an almost perfect circle of trees, most of
them burly elms of indeterminable age. There are also stumps and fallen trunks
of dead trees; one of them is so thick that even the tallest of Men would have
trouble putting his arms around it. A small pool of water has formed on the
bottom of a depression on the western slope at the edge of the wood; there might
be a spring nearby.
name: A Circle of Trees

desc:
Solitary, tall pines, standing above the field of moss and lichen here, do not
offer much shelter against the sun or the rain. The ground is sandy and dry, and
the only plants thriving here seem to be the heathers, which grow in thick
clusters covering the roots of the pines. Old stumps sticking out of the ground
here and there are grey, probably ant-infested, and seem to break apart easily.
name: A Dry Heath

desc:
Oblong bushes, many of them taller than Men, shade the slopes and hillsides with
their foliage. Some of the slopes are so steep that anyone would have
difficulties climbing on them, but it is not hard to find a twisting route
amidst the shrubbery to lead around the most difficult spots. Bird droppings
cover the ground under some of the cliff tops that are hardest to reach; perhaps
these are nesting grounds for eagles or hawks.
name: A Bushy Hillside

desc:
This slope separates the heathlands in the southeast from the plains below.
Climbing along the slope is hard; the paths leading past large boulders and
moss-covered outcrops of rock are impassable in many places, while loose peat
and moisture make the ground slippery. Slender rowans grow in the few places
where trees can easily take root; most of the slope remains barren, even though
water is trickling through the cracks in the cliff.
name: A Rugged Slope

desc:
Far more akin to a track than to a road, this old trail takes a corner here,
bending to the north and the east. By the side of the track stand a few,
long-dead trees that apparently provide a resting spot for the local birdlife.
Other than those dead trees, only some tough, grey-green grasses and the
occasional juniper bush grow here.
name: Bend in the Trail

desc:
A few, old logs have been dragged here by someone not too long ago, creating a
makeshift camp. A heap of old coals that once were a camp fire is still lying
around. East of here, one can discern a trail or track of some sort. South of
here, a plain that stretches out for long while. However, the plain looks as if
it has been split into two different elevations; a higher eastern part and a
lower western part.
name: Plains

desc:
This place bears the marks of significant geological upheavals that took place
aeons ago. Some unthinkable force has somehow managed to crack the plain open,
and an escarpment has risen out along the fault line. Looking south, one can see
a reddish rock wall rising out of the plain along the fault. The wall appears to
continue for miles and miles.
name: A Fault

desc:
Tough weeds, hardy bushes and withered rocks dominate this rugged plain. One
would be safe to assume that this is truly untouched wilderness. If there were
any settlers here once, they would soon have been driven away by the obvious
lack of water, fertile soil and security. At least the road that runs north from
here can provide the traveller with a route to more enjoyable destinations.
name: Rough Plain

desc:
Quite a sharp rise, this ridge-line overlooks the vast and forlorn plain west of
here. Far to the west, the Misty Mountains can barely be discerned as a haze at
the horizon. The vegetation here is quite sparse: only a few, tough grasses and
the occasional briar or shrub cling to the reddish earth that comprises this
field.
name: Beginning of a Ridge

desc:
Whereas the rock wall that looms east of here appears quite unclimbable, it
looks as though it declines both in height and steepness north of here.
Westwards, a rolling, grassy plain stretches out towards a faraway forest. At
this spot, however, only a sharp, tough, grey-green grass manages to thrive.
name: Plains by the Escarpment

desc:
Looking south or west, one sees only a long and reddish cliff wall that rises
out of the plain along what must be a geological fault line. Vegetation-wise,
this field hosts a few, hardy grasses and bushes. Along the very edge of the
cliff wall, pockets of water must have gathered at times, since one still can
see old animal tracks among the moist and muddy patches of clay.
name: Plains by the Escarpment

desc:
Here, the soft, reddish rock face of the escarpment sustains quite a large patch
of ivy that covers a sizeable part of the wall. Some juniper bushes crouch at
the base of the rock face. In all directions save east, a rolling country
unfolds, here and there dotted with clumps of darkish forests.
name: Plains by the Escarpment

desc:
The scant vegetation that grows here is mostly comprised by tough grey-green
grasses and tough-looking waist-high juniper bushes. The austere plains are
interrupted by a sheer cliff wall that drops down onto a lower field west of
here.
name: Escarpment on the Plain

desc:
A drop in the plain west of here makes travel in that direction impossible.
However, the sloping ridge here offers easy passage to the rolling grasslands in
other directions. The great fields reach out towards what must be the mighty
river Anduin far, far to the west.
name: Escarpment on the Plain

desc:
A handful of man-sized boulders rise out of this infertile plain, contributing
to the eerie appearance of this dusty patch of land. Confusingly enough, the
boulders look nothing like the harsh reddish ground: the pinnacles are of a dead
grey hue. Upon further inspection, one can discern almost humanoid features
among the withered pillars.
name: Strange Pinnacles

desc:
The reddish earth that comprises these plains appears unable to sustain any
vegetation apart from the thick grass and low bushes that surround the site.
Thus, it is a feast for the eyes to look up from the dust and gaze westward
towards the mighty Anduin. The great river can barely be discerned far to the
west, and even further west, a jagged line that can only be the highest peaks of
the Misty Mountains rises above the horizon.
name: Reddish Plains

desc:
While the western bank of this wide part of the Anduin is just another flat,
marshy plain, the eastern one is wooded and bordered by a thin layer of fallen
leaves. It is, however, slightly above the normal water level, and that keeps
the base of the trees safe from the river.
name: The Anduin River

desc:
Making a slow turn to the west the river heads straight for the Gladden Fields.
The landscape around is soggy, filled with pools of water and to the west a mist
is forming a few feet above the ground. From the shore long grey straws of grass
bend down in the water, touching its surface with their tips. From the muddy
bottom of the current other plants peek up in greeting.
name: Gently Flowing Anduin

desc:
The Anduin continues here on its rough path towards the southwest. While the
bottom of its wide bed is muddy and sluggish, the surrounding riverbanks are
rather flat plains. A small forest can be distinguished, beyond a couple of mild
bushes that are in growth on the eastern side.
name: The Anduin River

desc:
As the water flows gently to the south, animals can take their daily drinks here
without risk of being swept away in the currents. An occasional tree branch,
most likely ripped away by the roaring floods in the north, flows slowly down
the river. The shores are lower and less steep here, and make for a possible
crossing for anyone wanting to travel through the streaming water.
name: Calming in the Anduin

desc:
Following the sharp turn west the river just made it now eases back onto the
original path south. The roaring madness of the river further north is calming
down here. Only occasional white swirls can be seen as the water hits a
concealed rock or tree trunk. To the west, the elsewhere so scattered trees form
a haven for themselves, growing closer and closer together. Beyond this weald
the marshy lands of Gladden Fields can be spotted under the mist.
name: Anduin Swirls

desc:
The Anduin stream takes a rather sharp turn to the west here. Gazing further
south the river quickly moves back to its original path though, heading south
through the green landscape. Anything entering the water would quickly be
dragged into the rushing waves in the centre of the flood, and then swept away.
name: Turn in the Anduin

desc:
In the centre of this stream water rages like it wanted to crush the white foam
on its own waves. Rocks and stones peek up from the sandy bottom, but never
break the surface. Their presence is still enough to upset the river. Small
trees grow close to the shore flourishing in the presence of the clear water.
name: Rapids of the Anduin

desc:
The river runs past a rocky outcrop in the east, slowly eating away the cliff.
Farther away in the south it meets a steep, grassy embankment and bends slightly
to the west. The bottom of the river is not visible here, but it should not be
too deep since some rocks are sticking out of the water near the cliffs.
Branches and dead trunks floating in the river have gathered into a tangle among
some of the largest ones.
name: The Anduin Passing a Steep Cliff

desc:
Clear water rushes furiously southwards, dragging with it everything that dares
to cross its path. Closer to the shore it calms down, but it still moves with
distinct determination. A low slope separates the water from the grassy fields
beyond; on these sides animals visit frequently to drink from the water.
name: Rushing Anduin

desc:
Bending back to its original path to the south the river stretches out, cutting
through the green landscape. Behind a couple of rocks peeking up from the bottom
of the river, shadows of resting fish reflect in the clear but disturbed
surface. The water flows quickly southwards carving its way down in the soft
earth, leaving the banks numerous feet high.
name: Southward Stretch of the Anduin

desc:
Here on the very border of the Gladden Fields the river makes a turn south
again, as if avoiding the marshy landscape. Following its path it becomes
obvious however that it cannot avoid it much longer. In this area the land is
covered in a gentle mist rising from the ground, and the fields on either side
of the current are drenched in moss and water. This was once the shores of a
great lake, but now looks more like the shores of a moss-filled sea, stretching
as far as the eye can see in the west.
name: Anduin Entering the Gladden Fields

desc:
A smooth layer of moss covers the soil and the large rocks sticking out of the
ground here. The vegetation gets dense towards a shady depression in the south,
while a field of hay extends to the west. No trees grow in this rocky area; only
thick ferns and the woody stems of short perennial shrubs rise above the
evergreen carpet of moss.
name: Rocky Ground Bordering the Moors

desc:
The ground here is wet and the thick weeds that did not make it through the last
winter are slowly rotting away, turning into yet another layer of peat. It seems
like there once was a pond here; a cluster of rushes is withering on the bottom
of a depression, where the carpet of moss makes a squelching sound as it sinks
under anything heavier than a rabbit. Shrubs with leathery, oblong leaves are
thriving in the fields surrounding the depression.
name: Low Moors

desc:
The lonely birches and pines here are surrounded by a widespread growth of
heather. On the ground, the tiny pink flowers fallen off the heathers have
rolled into small piles and turned mostly brown. The dry needles and sticks
rustle quietly around anything moving through these heathlands, and the knocking
sounds of a woodpecker can be heard at times somewhere in the distance.
name: Patches of Heather

desc:
The sandy ground is tightly packed up by the roots of various bushes and plants
with woody stems growing here. The slope is steepest down in the north, where
the heath seems to continue as far as the eye can see, but there are also some
dangerous-looking spots on the rocky slope in the west. Stumps, mounds and other
odd shapes lie amidst the tangled undergrowth; clear paths are scarce here.
name: Sloping Heathlands

desc:
Harsh ground to the west slowly gives way to a more hospitable environment.
Scattered shrubs grow in sporadic clusters, while traces of heather intermingle
with other wild flowers. The ground itself is a mixture of sand and rich farming
soil. Aside from a make-shift trail that serves no apparent purpose, the land
seems mostly unaltered from its natural state. A faint path leads from a ruined
building in the east to a cottage in the north.
name: Edge of a Heath

desc:
A small field of gravel has formed into this hollow, surrounded by tall pines at
the edge of the heathlands. The source of the gravel seems to be at the hillside
in the south, where the roots of the trees and bushes growing on the slope have
failed to stop a landslide. Some dying trunks, brought down by the rolling
gravel, are lying on the bottom of the hollow while drying up and dropping their
last leaves one by one. A high hill rises above the heath in the south, but
climbing that way might be even harder than it looks.
name: A Gravel Pit

desc:
This is the highest point in this chain of hilltops stretching out to the east
and west, yet there are no good places to see far into the heathlands below.
Pine trees rise high above the ground here, and even their lowest branches seem
unreachable, while younger saplings are sprouting out of the sandy ground among
tussocks of grass. One must be careful while walking around here, for there are
rolling pine nuts and burly roots above the ground everywhere. Despite the
elevated location, even some flowering plants that normally do not thrive in
windy locations can be found on the slopes among the trees.
name: A High Hill

desc:
Rocky hills dominate the horizon, yet lower ground lies to the north and east of
here. The curvature of this landscape seems to act as a natural wind tunnel,
creating gustier conditions than one would expect. Scattered across the hills
are various types of pine trees, creating homes for small birds and animals.
Most low level foliage is scarce and sure footing is a rarity. To the west the
slope moves upward as it reaches its unimpressive apex.
name: Blustering Hills

desc:
Old and pitiful pine trees dot the area, reaching great heights but lacking many
branches. The grass here seems especially weathered, perhaps a result of high
winds coming from the south. Occasional shrubs grow between the grasses, though
it is difficult to tell if they are dead or alive.
name: Foot of the Blustering Hills

desc:
At the centre of these lightly wooded surroundings stands a small cottage, which
appears to have been abandoned some time ago. It is made completely of rough
stone except for the primitive wooden door which barely sticks out through the
thick overgrowth. Jutting up from the roof, a small chimney points to the sky.
Five long, flat rocks create steps leading up to the humble abode.
name: Abandoned Cottage

desc:
The rough stones forming the walls of this cottage are covered with thick layers
of moss. The front door, still sturdy despite the very damp air and deep dents
carved by sharp blades, provides an effective closure to the outside world.
Remains of furniture and household items are scattered on the floor, while in
the far corner various bones, some probably humanoid of origin, lie partly
covered between some ragged clothing.
name: Inside a Cottage

desc:
The ground is soft and squishy underfoot. Creeping fig has taken over the
majority of this soft landscape, creating a beautiful dark green blanket of
small round leaves. A few young cottonwoods struggle to break free from the
foliage. To the south an old cottage can be spotted.
name: Blanketed Meadows

desc:
This field is covered with wide expanses of grass and flowers without any
obstructions for large animals or humanoids. Hoofprints of those animals
visiting these abundant fields during wet days have been captured in the muddy
soil. On the lower somewhat sheltered grounds leaves litter the ground, dwarfing
tiny ants that carry them.
name: Grassy Plains

desc:
Starting from the farmstead which stands in the east, these fields show a
variety of crops; carrots, potatoes and cabbage are all growing here. Among the
fields you can see one that lies fallow revealing the rich, black soil
characteristic of the farms found in this area. A wooden fence separates the
most western fields from the edge of a ravine.
name: Vegetable Fields

desc:
The cultivated rye fields are separated by low earthen walls. The rye grows over
a foot high, with the occasional blue flower popping up here and there. Some
small tracks lead through the dense fields to a partly overgrown trail in the
east. A wooden fence prevents careless animals or others from walking over the
edge of the fields onto a pile of loose rocks leading into a deep crevice.
name: Rye Fields

desc:
This small yard, with here and there a tussock of low grass, ends at a wooden
barn to the north and a small house to the south. Near the barn, within an
enclosure of wooden poles, some pigs enjoy the mud, while at the other end a
large pile of wood, chopped into small blocks is placed against the wall of the
small house. From the west the smell of decomposing plants enters the yard,
while to the east the yard continues.
name: Farmyard

desc:
The trail ends in an open space with a small house to the south. The space
itself is covered in dust with here and there a tussock of grass or a lonely
weed. A shallow water-well, covered with a reed thatched roof, has been erected
in the southeastern corner of the yard. This well provides the local
inhabitants, their domesticated animals and the seedbeds with young vegetables
ready to be replanted in surrounding fields with water.
name: Open Space

desc:
A trail worn by the passage of both humans and animals passes through the
plains. Nevertheless, recent tracks are scarce and small shrubs and bushes grow
in different spots along it. The trail runs along a gentle slope from the
harvested fields to the west towards small copse of trees to the east.
name: Old Trail

desc:
The trail, completely covered by long thick grass approximately three feet tall,
bends from a northward to a westward direction, avoiding the marsh to the south.
East of the trail young willow trees, with thin straight branches emerging from
their knotted crowns, grow in unnaturally straight lines.
name: Bend in an Overgrown Trail

desc:
Sparse brush covers the terrain here, providing shelter and maintenance to
myriad smaller animals. An overgrown and seldom used trail is all that is left
between the stones bordering once a wide path. Little evidence is left of anyone
using this route at all, save for the remains of a small camp site. However,
northwards and westwards cultivated fields are the sign of recent human activity
in this area.
name: Bend in the Overgrown Trail

desc:
The fields are covered with regular spaced stumps of agriculture products like
corn and wheat, with deep tracks of wheels marking the places where carts stood
to load the harvested crops. On the ground mice run around collecting and eating
the leftovers, while in the sky birds spying for prey circle around. To the
north a low earthen wall covered with shrubs blocks the passage.
name: Harvested Fields

desc:
A small but well-maintained and well-furnished house features a big, warm
fireplace with deer pelts around it. Dried leaves are used to decorate the
windows. Around the room various baskets, at different stages of completion, lie
about. A workbench with typical basket weaver tools is placed beneath one of the
windows. A screen partially blocks the way to an area in the back of the house.
name: Basketmaker's House

desc:
This small room is separated from the main part of the house by a screen. A
large, brown fur covers most of the floor and the walls were constructed using
thick wooden beams. A small window shuttered by wooden planks provides the room
with some daylight. A pile of old, dusty clothes has been piled up in the far
corner of the room, and a sturdy bed is placed under the small window.
name: Basketmaker's Bedroom

desc:
Small windows made in the thick wooden walls enable the sunlight to penetrate to
the inside of the building. In the corner near the stove hams are hanging on
iron hooks, which in turn hang from the straw-thatched roof. The floor is
covered with baked red tiles, except for the cellar door. Some furniture,
obviously old, is placed in the house.
name: Farm House

desc:
Built underneath one of the buildings from the farm, this basement seems to
serve as some kind of storage facility. Wooden planks, filled with jars, have
been attached to the stone walls. Some of the jars have yellowish labels on them
describing their contents. The floor is mostly unoccupied except for a large
wooden chest in the far corner. A hatch with a ladder leads to the house above.
name: Musty Cellar

desc:
This large wooden barn is sectioned into several compartments by low wooden
walls. The back compartments are filled with piles of rye. Those more to the
front contain baskets with vegetables like carrots and cabbage, while the front
one, left of the entrance is equipped with a crib and a trough filled with
water. Right of the entrance a wooden bench with various tools, like sickle and
pitchfork, hanging next to it, marks the workroom of the local farmer.
name: Wooden Barn

desc:
The soft ground is covered by green plants and tall grasses. A row of huge logs
covered with mosses separates the fields from the path in the south. Dark
bushes, covered with small black berries grow at the eastern edge of the fields,
while some of the plants in the middle of the field seem to hide some sort of
vegetable under it. To the east the fields come to an abrupt ending at a very
deep and quite wide crevice.
name: Untamed Fields

desc:
The surrounding area seems to be quite flat, allowing a broad view. A beaten
path ending at a steep slope leading down is surrounded by small plants and grey
stones. There are a few bushes to the north and south,impeding travel somewhat
in these directions. To the west three ropes forming a very simple bridge span a
deep crevice.
name: Trail near a Deep Crevice

desc:
These grasslands south of an overgrown trail are rich with flowers and insects.
Small holes, not larger in diameter than the size of worm, with tiny piles of
black earth beside them, suggest recent underground activity in the fertile
soil. To the south, the bare soil appears even darker than usual, while to the
west the ground simply vanishes.
name: Grassy Plains

desc:
The earth rises here with a few barely noticeable hills. At a secluded part the
soil is suspiciously black and rich with compost. Its lack of crop or any other
sort of plant indicate something must have been harvested here in the recent
past. Jutting from the earth at the centre of the grasslands stands a boulder
reaching about three feet tall. In the lee of the stone to the south, a
makeshift shelter has been constructed. Some black corn cobs lie spread around a
recently burned-out camp fire.
name: Black Soil Grasslands

desc:
The ground here seems lower than the surrounding areas. Assorted grasses create
little patches of green here and there. Small clusters of purple and white wild
flowers dot the ground and provide a sweet scent to the air. To the east, a dark
patch of bare soil scars the grasslands, while to the north a deep crevice
blocks the way.
name: Dipped Grasslands

desc:
Soft, rolling fields of tall grass dominate most of this area. Very little can
be heard except the cooing of a few doves in the distance. The fragile grass
provides the wind a blank canvas, painting its every movement across the golden
fields. To the north a deep crevice blocks the way.
name: Tranquil Plains

desc:
Dominating the surroundings are what looks like the charred remains of a dense,
brush-filled flatland. An apparent brush fire must have swept through the area
recently, undoubtedly killing the plants and small animals alike. A number of
blackened stumps rise a few feet into the air with no hope of ever bearing new
growth again. Gusts of wind have blown ash through the air and most lies towards
a narrow crevice in the north.
name: Charred Brush

desc:
The uneven grassland is filled with small cracks and crevices, as if something
violent tried to reshape the landscape. In some of the moist cracks, wild
orchids can be seen within the green surroundings. To the east the grassland
ends at a rock slide, leading down into a crevice that is dozens of yards wide
and quite many feet deep.
name: Grasslands near a Crevice

desc:
A small ruin constructed of rough grey stones stands between the fig and vines.
The walls are overgrown with ivy and other plants, suggesting that it has been
in disrepair for a long long time already. Some old rotten planks fill an
opening which once used to be the entrance. Behind these boards, dense bushes
fill the the whole interior. Around the shack, rough fields continue in all
directions.
name: Overgrown Ruin

desc:
The meadow here has been completely enveloped in a rich, green blanket of
low-lying fig. The vines seem healthy and vast, stretching for miles to the
north and south. Moisture seems to stay trapped under the dense leaves, keeping
the ground below soft and cool; an ideal environment for bugs and spiders. An
old set of wooden fence posts have almost succumbed to the vines, with just
their tips appearing above the thick foliage.
name: Blanketed Meadows

desc:
The ground here seems especially soft, but it is unclear if that is due to the
thick foliage or soft ground below the fallen leaves. The slightly rolling hills
are almost completely consumed by a low-lying creeping fig. A slight stench
rises from the ground, indicating the recent death of something small hidden
beneath the leaves. Close to the west stands a petrified tree, grasping at the
sky with its claw-like branches.
name: Blanketed Meadows

desc:
The surrounding plots of lands appear to have been lush and green in the past,
but now only bald stems and trunks, filled with small holes from termites, are
left from that era. The former spring is covered with a hard crust of mud in
which here and there a skeleton of a fish or small animal has been trapped. The
mud spreads a malodorous smell over the surrounding plains.
name: Dried Out Spring

desc:
The path, leading to an old hut in the west, is marked with granite stones,
which are mostly hidden under huge piles of leaves. The raised northern and
southern edges of the path shelter it from strong winds. To the east it ends at
the edge of a crevice. However, a flimsy bridge constructed out of three ropes
spans the crevice, enabling travel to the other side.
name: End of an Overgrown Trail

desc:
Broken-up farmland stretches in all directions. The dark and nutrient-rich soil
shows itself through the occasional break in the rye patches. Riding uniformly
along the western edge of the fields stand dozens of old fence posts. They may
once have prevented unwanted wildlife to this area, but now decomposition has
robbed them of their rails. To the east a deep crevice blocks passage to the
plains beyond it.
name: Abandoned Rye Fields

desc:
Stretching all around are abandoned fields with here and there a small patch of
rye. Though it looks as if it could have been productive land, all that remains
are a few rusty, corroded tools and an old steel plough half buried in the
ground. To the east, on the other side of the crevice, some cultivated fields
are visible.
name: Abandoned Farmland

desc:
The ground slants slightly to the northeast before ending at a deep ravine. The
once groomed fiels are now overgrown by wild weeds and other brush. A large part
of this vegetation has dried, which indicates the water that can be heard
dripping inside the ravine is not available for plants on the surface. At some
miles distance in the west a small open spot in the landscape can be spotted.
name: Slanted Fields

desc:
The bottom of the crevice is littered with small pieces of slate which are
covered with imprints of fern leaves. Streams of water drip from the eastern
rock face forming a small stream which disappears to the south beneath the loose
rocks.
name: A Dark, Narrow Crevice

desc:
The floor of the crevice is covered with loose rocks originating from the
eastern side. This eastern rock face has partly collapsed forming a huge rock
slide of sharp edged rocks which enables travelling in and out of the crevice by
a skilled climber. The occasional fern grows near the eastern wall which
consists of layers of slate on top of solid granite. The crevice stretches for
miles in the northward and southward directions.
name: A Rockslide in a Crevice

desc:
The crevice is bordered by overhanging rock walls to the west and east. The
bottom is covered with some huge boulders between which ferns and other shade
loving plants have found a habitat. A dried out hide of a snake is stuck on one
of the sharp edges of the boulders. To the south the crevice looks greener as if
water has found its way there.
name: Crevice

desc:
The bottom of the crevice is partly hidden beneath a pool of murky water with
reeds and ferns growing on its banks. Some beetles and salamanders and some
bubbles which emit a faint sulphurous smell disturb the surface. High above the
pool three ropes, forming a bridge, span the crevice from east to west.
name: Crevice beneath a Rope Bridge

desc:
The bottom of the crevice is shaded by the overhanging walls. The bedrock is
covered with a thin layer of sand coming from the sediment layers in the rock
faces, and loose rocks with sharp edges broken from the lower granite layers.
The yellow sand consists of thousands and thousands of tiny fossil skeletons of
primitive creatures. Northwards the crevice grows deeper.
name: Shaded Crevice

desc:
Various bones of large animals lie scattered between the numerous sharp rocks
that cover the solid bedrock.. The hollows between those rocks have been filled
with dirt originating from the grasslands around. Pioneer species like greater
plantain and common horsetail add some green to the otherwise grey landscape. To
the west a rock slide filling the crevice makes it possible scramble up to the
grasslands.
name: Rock Slide

desc:
A weather-beaten trail running north to south can still be clearly seen,
nevertheless time-worn and faded tracks are evidence of little, if any, recent
traffic. To the north, in the distance, a small farm can be distinguished. To
the west some field, the uses of which cannot be determined from this distance,
fill the horizon.
name: Fading Trail

desc:
As the curvy trail continues from north to west, one can see a little path,
probably made by animals leading southwards. The trail, originally covered with
some small pieced gravel, is now mostly overgrown by low grasses and weeds.
Beside the trail an old log, providing a view of the marshy grasslands to the
east, is placed like a bench.
name: Curve in an Overgrown Trail

desc:
Man made ditches, filled with a few feet of water, cut through the wetlands,
dividing it into long stretches of floating mats of vegetation. On one of these
mats a small shelter, with a view across a small lake, has been constructed out
of rough wooden poles and braided twigs. Near the trail to the northwest some
small piles of dark brown peat have been placed, ready for transportation.
name: Wetlands

desc:
Some bushes and small trees grow here. Among these a few patches of thistles and
some scattered ground-level thrive. Around the flourishing bushes a number of
small birds fly around, picking up the occasional insect hiding between the
leaves. The ground gradually slopes down toward a small pond to the south. Some
winding animal tracks head in that direction.
name: Field by a Pond

desc:
Over time a small depression has developed in these grasslands. Rainwater from
the surrounding fields drains to there forming a large, tranquil pond. This pond
has a distinctive green colour from algae that exists among the water- lilies
growing along the shoreline. Despite being surrounded by reeds a small small
path leading to the waterfront, can be distinguished.
name: Pond in the Fields

desc:
The fields here are overgrown with thistles, shrubs and bushes. Standing in the
middle of the fields, the weather-beaten remains of an old building can be seen.
An old, fading trail leads from the village remains to the east, across the
fields and down the gentle westward slope to a small pond.
name: Overgrown Fields

desc:
An open plain stretches from east to west, bordered in the north by some lone
birch trees in a soggy loam. The plain provides little in the form of shelter
from the elements or predators. Nevertheless, faint trails of animal tracks,
most likely deer, criss-cross through the open landscape.
name: Plains

desc:
The soggy nature of these wetlands makes it hard to keep balance. The surface,
consisting of mosses, has a healthy light green look, apart from the places
where the water level has risen above the vegetation. At the places where the
ground is more solid thick patches of grass and some solitary birch and willow
trees grow. To the west, at higher grounds, a trail can be spotted.
name: Wetlands near a Trail

desc:
The bridge, which is constructed out of three ropes, spans the crevice from west
to east allowing a somewhat safe route from one side of the crevice to the other
side. The thickest rope hangs several feet lower than the other two thinner
ones. Far below the ropes a murky pool covers the base of the crevice.
name: Rope Bridge

desc:
This small lodge had been erected by stacking thick wooden beams on top of each
other. A heavy wooden door marks its entrance, while a small window with
shutters gives a great view over the long crevice in the south. The interior of
this home consists of some simple furniture with a few paintings of farm animals
attached to the walls.
name: Herder's Lodge
